title: 7 Lessons From My 2:49 Marathon (That Have Nothing To Do With Running) o-with-running
author: Sahil Bloom
summary: Sahil Bloom reports that six days after missing his marathon goal he ran the course alone at dawn and finished in 2:48:47. He then shares seven lessons from the training that apply well beyond running. These include progressive overload, visualizing the work instead of the outcome, laying one brick at a time, pacing a long race conservatively, tracking inputs, bundling a want with a should, and never betting against the person who keeps showing up. Each lesson is anchored in a story or study, such as Milo of Croton, Will Smith's brick wall and Katy Milkman's temptation bundling research. The through-line is that patient, consistent effort compounds over time, and that the person who shows up through the unrewarded valley wins.
points: Progressive overload applies to focus, resilience and skill as much as to strength, and progress is returns to the power of time.
Visualizing the end result can drain drive, so it is better to picture yourself doing the daily work.
Careers, health and relationships are marathons that cannot be won in the early miles but can be lost by burning out early.
Tracking inputs separated the goals Bloom achieved from those he missed over the last decade.
Temptation bundling, pairing something you want with something you should do, made his dreaded weekly long run something to look forward to.
quotes: You can never bet against the person who just keeps showing up.
Remember: Progress is returns to the power of time. Time is the exponent. What matters isn't the growth in any given week. But the amount of time you stack it for.
Visualizing the end outcome before you've done the work to earn it can actually trick your brain into feeling a premature sense of accomplishment.
It doesn't have to be impressive. In fact, most days, it won't look or feel impressive. But if you keep showing up and laying one brick with focus, you'll eventually build that wall.
Every meaningful "race" in life is a long game. Your career. Your health. Your relationships. They're each quite literally the equivalent of a marathon.

But most people stop when it's none of those things. Few have the courage to keep showing up through the valley.
